VIDEO.title: Matthew 15:1-28 – Jesus EXPOSED This Church Tradition…
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: This people honors Me with their lips, but their heart is far away from Me.
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 15:1-28. Pharisees and scribes come from Jerusalem and ask why Jesus' disciples break the tradition of the elders by not washing their hands. Jesus answers with a question: why do they transgress God's commandment for their tradition? Their rule about gifts 'given to God' lets a son avoid honoring his parents. He quotes Isaiah 29:13, teaches that what defiles comes from the heart, and calls them blind guides. Then in the district of Tyre and Sidon a Canaanite woman's great faith wins healing for her daughter.

The exchange starts out cordial; it turns contentious when Jesus calls them hypocrites. Their tradition is halakha, rules for how to walk out the Law in unclear cases. The video gives a Mishnah example about a poor man at the door on the Sabbath.

Corban (Mark 7:11) let a child declare goods set aside for God and so refuse them to needy parents, voiding the command to honor father and mother (Exodus 20:12; 21:17; Deuteronomy 5:16). Like Hosea 6:6, which Jesus quoted twice before, Isaiah 29 shows God wants hearts close to Him.

Israel was God's planting (Isaiah 60:21; Ezekiel 17:22-24; 16:7); plants He did not plant will be uprooted. 'Blind guides' recalls Isaiah 56:10 and Malachi 2:8. What defiles is what comes out of the heart; Mark adds pride (Mark 7:22). The Canaanite woman is an intentional contrast.

The lesson: beware the heart behind religious customs or traditions. If the heart behind the tradition is defiled, the tradition will violate God's word. The video then asks how a church can test its own traditions.
QUOTES: Why does a Jewish rabbi answer a question with a question? Why not?
Beware the heart behind religious customs or traditions.
If the heart behind the tradition is defiled, the tradition will violate God's word.
This is no accident, ladies and gentlemen.

method.p: The teacher reads the Canaanite woman as an intentional contrast with the Pharisees and scribes just before. Set the two scenes side by side and compare who comes, what they ask, and how Jesus answers.

LSB_QUOTES.text: You hypocrites, rightly did Isaiah prophesy of you: ‘This people honors Me with their lips, / But their heart is far away from Me.
But the things that proceed out of the mouth come from the heart, and those defile the man.
Then Jesus answered and said to her, “O woman, your faith is great; it shall be done for you as you wish.” And her daughter was healed at once.

src.text: Then some Pharisees and scribes *came to Jesus from Jerusalem and said, “Why do Your disciples break the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread.” And He answered and said to them, “Why do you yourselves transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition?

lines.text: They came all the way from Jerusalem. So far the exchange is above board and fairly cordial; it turns contentious when Jesus calls them hypocrites (15:7).
Luke records a Pharisee who marveled that Jesus 'had not first ceremonially washed before the meal' (Luke 11:38).
The tradition of the elders is halakha, from a word meaning 'to walk': rules for how to keep the Law in cases where it did not seem clear how to obey it.

The video's example: Deuteronomy 15 says to open your hand to the poor, and Exodus 20:10 says to rest on the Sabbath. What if a poor man comes on the Sabbath? The video describes a Mishnah case where giving across the doorway, with neither stepping through, keeps the Sabbath.
The rabbis described the tradition as handed down from Moses and said, 'make a fence round the Torah' (Pirkei Avot 1:1).

left.text: For God said, ‘Honor your father and mother,’ and, ‘He who speaks evil of father or mother is to be put to death.’

right.text: but you say, ‘If a man says to his father or his mother, whatever you might benefit from me is Corban (that is to say, given to God),’

lines.text: Honoring parents meant caring for them in need. The video says the rule let a son or daughter declare valuables set aside for the temple, to be given after their death, and so refuse to help their parents.
Jesus quotes the Law to show the clear duty of children to care for their parents: Exodus 20:12, Exodus 21:17 and Deuteronomy 5:16.
The Mishnah lists 'konam' as a substitute for 'korban' in vows (Mishnah Nedarim 1:2), and the rabbis allowed a vow harming parents to be dissolved (Mishnah Nedarim 9:1).

left.text: ‘This people honors Me with their lips, / But their heart is far away from Me. / But in vain do they worship Me, / Teaching as doctrines the commands of men.’

right.text: Then the Lord said, / “Because this people draw near with their mouth / And honor Me with their lips, / But they remove their hearts far from Me, / And their fear of Me is in the command of men learned by rote,

lines.text: Jesus' train of thought tracks His earlier quotes of Hosea 6:6 (9:13; 12:7): God desires mercy that reveals a heart close to Him, which the Pharisees and scribes lack.

src.text: After Jesus called the crowd to Him, He said to them, “Hear and understand. It is not what enters into the mouth that defiles the man, but what proceeds out of the mouth, this defiles the man.”

lines.text: The video applies 'what comes out of the mouth' to the Pharisees' own teaching, the oral rules. In seeking to remain pure, they disengaged from the very things God wants them to do.
Halakha that comes from a right reading of God's word looks like what Jesus did: eat with sinners, heal the sick, feed the hungry, help the needy, cast out demons, often on the Sabbath.

HEART.title: Plants the Father did not plant

left.text: But He answered and said, “Every plant which My heavenly Father did not plant shall be uprooted.

right.text: Then all your people will be righteous; / They will possess the land forever, / The branch of My planting, / The work of My hands, / That I may show forth My beautiful glory.

lines.text: In many places Israel is pictured as a plant, a vine or a tree (Isaiah 60:21; Ezekiel 17:22-24; Ezekiel 16:7), until Jesus calls Himself the true vine (John 15:1).

left.text: Let them alone; they are blind guides of the blind. And if a blind man guides a blind man, both will fall into a pit.”

right.text: His watchmen are blind; / All of them know nothing. / All of them are mute dogs unable to bark, / Dreamers lying down, who love to slumber;

lines.text: The Lord condemns Israel's corrupt leaders and priests for turning aside and causing many to stumble by their instruction (Malachi 2:8).
You will recognize such teachers by the kind of teaching they teach and the students they produce (Matthew 7:15-21).

src.text: But the things that proceed out of the mouth come from the heart, and those defile the man. For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, sexual immoralities, thefts, false witness, slanders. These are the things which defile the man; but to eat with unwashed hands does not defile the man.”

lines.text: 'Are you still lacking in understanding also?' (15:16). Mark's list includes pride (Mark 7:22), a corrupt desire flowing straight from the heart.
The lesson: beware the heart behind religious customs or traditions. If the heart behind the tradition is defiled, the tradition will violate God's word.

src.text: And going away from there, Jesus withdrew into the district of Tyre and Sidon. And behold, a Canaanite woman from that region came out and began to cry out, saying, “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David; my daughter is cruelly demon-possessed.”

lines.text: Right after the leaders from Jerusalem, Jesus meets a Gentile. This is no accident: the exchange is an intentional contrast with the one before.
Mark calls her 'a Greek, of Syrophoenician descent' (Mark 7:26). Matthew's 'Canaanite' recalls Israel's old enemies, yet she calls Jesus 'Son of David.'

src.text: But He did not answer her a word. And His disciples came and were pleading with Him, saying, “Send her away, because she keeps shouting at us.” But He answered and said, “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”

lines.text: Jesus said the same when He sent out the Twelve (10:5-6). After the resurrection He sends them to all the nations (28:19).

src.text: And He answered and said, “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” But she said, “Yes, Lord; but even the dogs feed on the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table.”

lines.text: The word is a diminutive, kynarion: a house dog, not a wild street dog. She takes His word and turns it into a plea.
Everything Jesus says and does with her reads against the Pharisees: they honored God with their lips; she bows down and cries, 'Lord, help me!'

src.text: Then Jesus answered and said to her, “O woman, your faith is great; it shall be done for you as you wish.” And her daughter was healed at once.

lines.text: The religious leaders, with all their tradition, are blind guides; the Gentile woman, with nothing but her trust, is praised for great faith.
Compare the centurion, another Gentile whose faith Jesus praised (8:10), and Elijah's widow of Zarephath in Sidon (1 Kings 17:9; Luke 4:26).

TERMS.def: The body of oral rules handed down to apply the Law; later written in the Mishnah.
From a word for 'to walk': the rules for how to live out the Law. The captions write 'hakic' and 'helocic.'
'An offering,' a vow formula declaring something given to God (Mark 7:11).
In Greek an actor; one whose outward show hides a different heart.
To make common or ritually unclean; Jesus locates defilement in the heart.
A hint back to an Old Testament passage; the captions write 'Rome.'
A Phoenician from the province of Syria, Mark's description of the woman (Mark 7:26). The captions write 'cyro phoenician.'

Little dog, house dog. Look up: BDAG, κυνάριον.
Corban, an offering given to God.
To be heavy; in the piel, to honor. Look up: BDB or HALOT, כבד.

BACKGROUND.p: Washing hands before eating was a matter of ritual purity, not hygiene. The Mishnah even sets the amount of water: 'a quarter [of a log] of water must be poured over the hands for one [person] and even for two' (Mishnah Yadayim 1:1).

The Mishnah traces the tradition from Moses to the Men of the Great Assembly, who said, 'make a fence round the Torah' (Pirkei Avot 1:1): extra rules to keep people far from breaking the commandments.

The rabbis prized this command too. The Mishnah lists 'Honoring one’s father and mother' among deeds whose fruit a man enjoys in this world while the principal remains for the world to come (Mishnah Peah 1:1).
The Phoenician port cities north of Galilee were wealthy Gentile centers that bought grain from Galilee. Jesus had already said they would have repented had they seen His works (11:21).

WITNESSES.text: But not the less were they innovating; as in this instance, that one ought not to eat with unwashen hands, that we must wash cups and brazen vessels, that we must wash also ourselves.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 51, on 15:2. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: And He said not, the elders' tradition, but your own.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 51, on 15:3. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 52, on 15:27. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

DEBATES.h: Did Jesus set aside the food laws?
DEBATES.p: Mark adds, 'Thus He declared all foods clean' (Mark 7:19). Matthew ends with handwashing (15:20). Some read Matthew as a ruling on the elders' tradition only; others see the same teaching as Mark's.

The video says goods were pledged to the temple after the giver's death. Others think the vow simply barred parents from benefiting, with the goods never actually given. The Mishnah shows later rabbis allowed such vows to be dissolved for the parents' sake (Mishnah Nedarim 9:1).

Some read Jesus as testing her faith; others as voicing the disciples' attitude to expose it; others as stating the order of His mission, 'to the Jew first.' All agree He grants her request and praises her faith.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video lists 'Leviticus 29' among the passages Jesus quotes. Leviticus has 27 chapters; the verse is Leviticus 20:9: 'If there is anyone who curses his father or his mother, he shall surely be put to death' (Leviticus 20:9).

The Mishnah case of the poor man at the door (Mishnah Shabbat 1:1) is about who is liable for carrying between domains on the Sabbath, not a rule for how to give to the poor. Where each does part of the act, 'both of them are exempt.'
That Corban goods went to the temple after the giver's death is one interpretation; the Gospels do not say so.
'To abolish means to misinterpret' is the video's view from an earlier episode, not a standard meaning of the Greek word in Matthew 5:17.
The captions write 'hakic,' 'hocic' and 'helocic' for halakhic, 'Ty and Sidon' for Tyre and Sidon, 'Exodus 2012' for Exodus 20:12, 'cyro phoenician' for Syrophoenician, and 'Rome' for remez.

QUESTIONS: What is a custom or tradition in your church, and what is the heart behind it?
How can a good rule end up voiding God's word? Can you think of an example?
Where might you honor God with your lips while your heart is far away?
Jesus says defilement comes from the heart. Which item in His list (or Mark's 'pride') do you most need to watch?
What stands out to you in the contrast between the leaders from Jerusalem and the Canaanite woman?
How does her persistence shape the way you pray?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson for Jesus' original audience: beware the heart behind religious customs or traditions. If the heart behind the tradition is defiled, the tradition will violate God's word. There are all kinds of implications, whether for Jesus' day or our own, but that is what Jesus wants His people to hear and understand. How do we know whether a tradition of our church violates God's word? We must be careful and investigate whether the customs and traditions of our local church reflect the heart of God. Customs and traditions are habitual ways of acting among a group; many churches have clearly delineated practices that are liturgical and have theological and doctrinal purposes, such as corporately affirming certain creeds. The question is not whether we have traditions, but whether the heart behind them is close to the Lord.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): pick one habit in your own worship, private or public. Ask what it is for, where it comes from in Scripture, and whether it helps you love God and neighbor or has become a way around them.

## The Canaanite woman
1. Matthew 15:21-22: A Canaanite woman
   Contrast Matthew 15:21-22: "And going away from there, Jesus withdrew into the district of Tyre and Sidon. And behold, a Canaanite woman from that region came out and began to cry out, saying, “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David; my daughter is cruelly demon-possessed.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+15:21-22
   (video) Right after the leaders from Jerusalem, Jesus meets a Gentile. This is no accident: the exchange is an intentional contrast with the one before.
   [Background] Mark calls her 'a Greek, of Syrophoenician descent' (Mark 7:26). Matthew's 'Canaanite' recalls Israel's old enemies, yet she calls Jesus 'Son of David.' (Mark 7:26)
2. Matthew 15:23-24: The lost sheep of Israel
   Silence Matthew 15:23-24: "But He did not answer her a word. And His disciples came and were pleading with Him, saying, “Send her away, because she keeps shouting at us.” But He answered and said, “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+15:23-24
   [Background] Jesus said the same when He sent out the Twelve (10:5-6). After the resurrection He sends them to all the nations (28:19). (Matthew 10:5-6; Matthew 28:19)
3. Matthew 15:25-27: Even the dogs
   Faith Matthew 15:26-27: "And He answered and said, “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” But she said, “Yes, Lord; but even the dogs feed on the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+15:26-27
   [Background] The word is a diminutive, kynarion: a house dog, not a wild street dog. She takes His word and turns it into a plea.
   (video) Everything Jesus says and does with her reads against the Pharisees: they honored God with their lips; she bows down and cries, 'Lord, help me!'
4. Matthew 15:28: Your faith is great
   Healed Matthew 15:28: "Then Jesus answered and said to her, “O woman, your faith is great; it shall be done for you as you wish.” And her daughter was healed at once." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+15:28
   (video) The religious leaders, with all their tradition, are blind guides; the Gentile woman, with nothing but her trust, is praised for great faith.
   [Background] Compare the centurion, another Gentile whose faith Jesus praised (8:10), and Elijah's widow of Zarephath in Sidon (1 Kings 17:9; Luke 4:26). (Matthew 8:10; 1 Kings 17:9)

## Key people
- Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem: Ask why the disciples break the tradition of the elders. [Background] Mark explains that the Pharisees 'and all the Jews' washed carefully before eating (Mark 7:3).
- The disciples: Worried that the Pharisees were offended; still lacking understanding. [Background] They will ask again about this teaching (Mark 7:17).
- Peter: Asks, 'Explain the parable to us.' [Background] Later God teaches Peter not to call anyone unclean (Acts 10:28).
- Isaiah: Prophesied of lips near and hearts far from God. [Background] Jesus says Isaiah 'rightly' prophesied of them (15:7).
- The Canaanite woman: An intentional contrast with the leaders; praised for great faith. [Background] Mark calls her a Syrophoenician Greek (Mark 7:26).
- Her daughter: Cruelly demon-possessed, healed at once. [Background] Mark says the woman went home and found the demon gone (Mark 7:30).

- Tyre (named in the video): Jesus withdrew 'into the district of Tyre and Sidon' (15:21).
- Zarephath: A village of Sidon where Elijah was sent to a widow (1 Kings 17:9), another Gentile woman blessed.
- Capernaum: Jesus' base in Galilee.

## Key terms
- Tradition of the elders: The body of oral rules handed down to apply the Law; later written in the Mishnah.
- Halakha: From a word for 'to walk': the rules for how to live out the Law. The captions write 'hakic' and 'helocic.'
- Corban: 'An offering,' a vow formula declaring something given to God (Mark 7:11).
- Hypocrite: In Greek an actor; one whose outward show hides a different heart.
- Defile: To make common or ritually unclean; Jesus locates defilement in the heart.
- Remez: A hint back to an Old Testament passage; the captions write 'Rome.'
- Syrophoenician: A Phoenician from the province of Syria, Mark's description of the woman (Mark 7:26). The captions write 'cyro phoenician.'

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Handwashing: Washing hands before eating was a matter of ritual purity, not hygiene. The Mishnah even sets the amount of water: 'a quarter [of a log] of water must be poured over the hands for one [person] and even for two' (Mishnah Yadayim 1:1).
- A fence around the Torah: The Mishnah traces the tradition from Moses to the Men of the Great Assembly, who said, 'make a fence round the Torah' (Pirkei Avot 1:1): extra rules to keep people far from breaking the commandments.
- Honoring parents: The rabbis prized this command too. The Mishnah lists 'Honoring one’s father and mother' among deeds whose fruit a man enjoys in this world while the principal remains for the world to come (Mishnah Peah 1:1).
- Tyre and Sidon: The Phoenician port cities north of Galilee were wealthy Gentile centers that bought grain from Galilee. Jesus had already said they would have repented had they seen His works (11:21).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Did Jesus set aside the food laws? Mark adds, 'Thus He declared all foods clean' (Mark 7:19). Matthew ends with handwashing (15:20). Some read Matthew as a ruling on the elders' tradition only; others see the same teaching as Mark's.
- How did Corban work? The video says goods were pledged to the temple after the giver's death. Others think the vow simply barred parents from benefiting, with the goods never actually given. The Mishnah shows later rabbis allowed such vows to be dissolved for the parents' sake (Mishnah Nedarim 9:1).
- Why the harsh word 'dogs'? Some read Jesus as testing her faith; others as voicing the disciples' attitude to expose it; others as stating the order of His mission, 'to the Jew first.' All agree He grants her request and praises her faith.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video lists 'Leviticus 29' among the passages Jesus quotes. Leviticus has 27 chapters; the verse is Leviticus 20:9: 'If there is anyone who curses his father or his mother, he shall surely be put to death' (Leviticus 20:9).
- The Mishnah case of the poor man at the door (Mishnah Shabbat 1:1) is about who is liable for carrying between domains on the Sabbath, not a rule for how to give to the poor. Where each does part of the act, 'both of them are exempt.'
- That Corban goods went to the temple after the giver's death is one interpretation; the Gospels do not say so.
- 'To abolish means to misinterpret' is the video's view from an earlier episode, not a standard meaning of the Greek word in Matthew 5:17.
- The captions write 'hakic,' 'hocic' and 'helocic' for halakhic, 'Ty and Sidon' for Tyre and Sidon, 'Exodus 2012' for Exodus 20:12, 'cyro phoenician' for Syrophoenician, and 'Rome' for remez.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. What is a custom or tradition in your church, and what is the heart behind it?
2. How can a good rule end up voiding God's word? Can you think of an example?
3. Where might you honor God with your lips while your heart is far away?
4. Jesus says defilement comes from the heart. Which item in His list (or Mark's 'pride') do you most need to watch?
5. What stands out to you in the contrast between the leaders from Jerusalem and the Canaanite woman?
6. How does her persistence shape the way you pray?

## Application
- (video) The lesson for Jesus' original audience: beware the heart behind religious customs or traditions. If the heart behind the tradition is defiled, the tradition will violate God's word. There are all kinds of implications, whether for Jesus' day or our own, but that is what Jesus wants His people to hear and understand. How do we know whether a tradition of our church violates God's word? We must be careful and investigate whether the customs and traditions of our local church reflect the heart of God. Customs and traditions are habitual ways of acting among a group; many churches have clearly delineated practices that are liturgical and have theological and doctrinal purposes, such as corporately affirming certain creeds. The question is not whether we have traditions, but whether the heart behind them is close to the Lord.
- Study note (added): pick one habit in your own worship, private or public. Ask what it is for, where it comes from in Scripture, and whether it helps you love God and neighbor or has become a way around them.
